title: Comparative analysis of protease-inhibitor gene family counts under different counting units and genome annotations
authors: Zhao, F.; Zhao, J.; Zhao, F.
abstract: Background: Gene family sizes are often compared across species using the protein sets released with genome assemblies. However, counts of domain-positive protein entries can differ from counts of genes when an annotation contains several entries per gene, and genomes are annotated by different pipelines. In this study, we measured how these two factors change the counts of protease-inhibitor domain families. Results: Seven protease-inhibitor families were counted in eight animal genomes. Collapsing protein entries to genes reduced the counts in 36 of 48 species-family combinations, by up to 4.6-fold (Kunitz/BPTI in Aedes aegypti, 23 entries in 5 genes), and reversed the order of two species in 9 of 196 pairwise comparisons. In 218 of 223 gene-family records with several positive entries, all entries shared CDS coordinates with the representative entry. Two annotations of the same leech (Hirudinaria manillensis) assembly differed in a family-specific way. In the published annotation, 38 of 50 Antistasin-positive genes and both Hirudin-positive genes had no same-strand gene model in a second annotation, whereas most Kunitz/BPTI, Serpin, TIL and Thyroglobulin genes had one-to-one partners. A search of the eight assemblies without gene models detected all 338 annotated Kunitz/BPTI-positive genes when the queries included proteins of the same species. Queries from other species recovered only 31-83% of these genes, and Kunitz-like candidate regions outside the annotations were most numerous in the tick Ixodes scapularis. For the mosquito and the tick, the second public annotations shared nearly all gene-model coordinates with RefSeq and were therefore excluded from the comparison of annotation sources. Conclusions: These results indicate that gene family counts depend on the counting unit and on the annotation source. Comparisons across species should count each gene once and state how domain positivity was assigned to genes. In addition, the source and version of each annotation should be reported, the annotations should be checked against the genome assembly, and the overlap of gene models should be examined before two annotations are compared.

title: VoroTIDE: Protein domain segmentation through independent hierarchical searches using Voronoi tessellation and physical self-containment
authors: Le, K. Q.
abstract: Protein domains are commonly regarded as structurally separated, functionally relevant, and evolutionarily separable units. Although classification systems may assign different domain boundaries to the same structure, structural separation remains a shared criterion, and many domain parsers assess it through inter-residue distances, contact numbers, or contact densities. However, the Voronoi contact area, which is widely used to study protein-protein interactions and predict contact sites, has seen limited use in domain parsing. There are two potential challenges to this problem. First, unlike in protein-protein interaction, partitions are not known in advance and must be identified before their interface can be evaluated. Second, the contact area depends on fragment size and internal packing, making it difficult to compare candidate partitions. Here, we introduce VoroTIDE (Voronoi-based Two-way Independent Domain Exploration), a domain parser based on all-heavy-atom Voronoi contact areas. By normalizing the contact area for fragment size and internal packing, and incorporating residue hydropathy, we define a pairwise self-containment score F. VoroTIDE applies F in two independent hierarchical searches: top-down recursive splitting until no admissible division remains, and bottom-up merging of secondary-structure elements until the entire structure becomes a single fragment. Intermediate partitions from both searches are ranked by a global partition quality score G, derived on the same principle. On two CATH-ECOD consensus benchmarks, under balanced evaluation, VoroTIDE achieved the strongest performance among all tested criterion-based parsers and was comparable to Chainsaw, the best-performing deep learning method tested. These results show that the Voronoi-based criterion can yield competitive domain parsing.

title: Integrative structure determination of a human mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system (MICOS) sub-assembly
authors: Jindal, M.; Mahato, R.; Das, S.; Guha, A.; Majila, K.; Arvindekar, S.; Vaidya, A. T.; Viswanath, S.
abstract: The Mitochondrial contact site and Cristae Organizing System (MICOS) complex is an inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) assembly present at the cristae junction. It is responsible for regulating cristae formation and remodeling. However, its structure is not known. We applied Bayesian integrative structure determination to characterize the structure of the Mic60, Mic19, Mic10, and Mic13-containing MICOS sub-assembly combining AlphaFold predictions with data from crosslinking mass spectrometry, biochemical assays, electron tomography, homology modeling, and sequence alignments. The integrative structure revealed novel mutual interfaces among Mic10N,C, Mic60LBS1,LBS2,mitofilin, and Mic13central,C. Several likely-pathogenic missense mutations also localize to these novel interfaces, highlighting their importance. Further, we investigated some of these interactions using binding assays on purified proteins and demonstrated direct interactions among Mic10-Mic13-Mic60. Our results support a bridging role for Mic13 in the MICOS assembly, by binding Mic10 in the IMM-proximal region and Mic60 in the intermembrane space. Taken together, our integrative approach sheds light on the structure and assembly of the MICOS complex.

title: Continuous, high-speed 3D topographic profiling of living tissue monolayers
authors: Shin, D.; Park, J.; Ahn, J.; Choi, A.; Kang, J. H.
abstract: Tissue monolayers are active living matter whose three-dimensional (3D) architecture and mechanical remodeling regulate tissue function, yet fast and continuous topographic monitoring remains difficult. Here, we present FLuorescence EXclusion microscopy fOr Monolayers (FLEXOM), a microfluidic platform that combines multilayer micropillar arrays with negative-staining optics to convert wide-field images into self-calibrated 3D height maps. Geometry-anchored reference cavities maintain in-frame calibration standards even in fully confluent monolayer fields, enabling continuous 3D profiling from isolated cells to confluent sheets with sub-second temporal resolution (~250 ms), sub-micrometer axial precision (~0.37 m), and multi-day biocompatibility and operational stability (>96 h). FLEXOM reveals two distinct anisotropic signatures in tissue monolayers. First, monolayers of different cell types show distinct vertical thickness profiles despite comparable lateral footprints. Only two vertical descriptors, mean height and height variability, distinguished cell types more accurately than nine 2D lateral descriptors, including area, circularity, and convexity (95% vs. 76%). Second, under acute osmotic shock, confluent monolayers exhibit geometrically anisotropic and temporally decoupled vertical-lateral remodeling: height changes dominate the overall volume response and precede lateral remodeling. Surprisingly, cyclic isotonic-hypotonic pulses every 3 min confine remodeling entirely to the vertical axis. Overall, our work provides a high-resolution 3D profiling tool and a framework for axis-resolved analysis of topographic responses in active living matter.

title: Somatostatin-excitatory coordination emerges with dexterous motor skill learning
authors: Wheeler Fox, G.; Wiener, E. T.; MacLean, J. N.
abstract: Motor skill-learning increases spatio-temporal consistency in neuronal activity in primary motor cortex (M1), and Somatostatin-expressing (SST) interneurons are causally involved in these learning-related activity changes. Yet, how SST-excitatory interactions shape population level activity changes during motor skill acquisition is still unknown. Here, we imaged large populations of excitatory neurons and identified SST or parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons across successive days as mice learned a dexterous, persistently M1-dependent reach-to-grasp task. Sparse, temporally coordinated, trial-resolved, and rate-controlled functional interactions between SST neurons and skill-modulated excitatory neurons emerged with learning and were stronger than those in excitatory-excitatory or PV-excitatory pairs. Interactions strengthened as neurons were recruited to the skill-modulated ensemble and weakened when skill modulation was lost. SST activity also became temporally reliable earlier than excitatory or PV activity, and SST consistency was significantly associated with behavioral performance even after controlling for training session number. Additionally, SST neurons carried more information about movement kinematics than randomly selected subsets of excitatory neurons. Overall, SST neurons became selectively coordinated with behaviorally relevant excitatory populations, revealing a cell-type-specific functional architecture for dexterous motor learning.

title: Differential endothelial cell remodeling in Down syndrome and APP duplication drives distinct blood brain barrier dysfunction
authors: Valay, L.; Kasri, A.; Fontaine, V.; Camporesi, E.; Bigou, S.; Brinkmalm, G.; Piotrowska, D.; Dancette, L.; Lamontagne, M.; Lejeune, F.-X.; Halder, P.; Ravassard, P.; Irmler, M.; Zetterberg, H.; Beckers, J.; Potier, M.-C.
abstract: An extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene (APP) is present in Down syndrome (DS) and APP duplication (APPdup), increasing the risk of Alzheimer disease (AD) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). However, we reported greater vascular A{beta} deposition in APPdup than in DS with AD, suggesting that other triplicated chromosome 21 genes may mitigate CAA severity. We investigated endothelial cell (EC) function and blood brain barrier (BBB) integrity in DS and APPdup using human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived ECs (iECs), assessing their morphology, junctional proteins, A{beta} peptide secretion, barrier function, and transcriptomic profiles. Both DS and APPdup iECs secreted more A{beta}40 A{beta}42 compared with their respective isogenic controls but exhibited distinct A{beta} peptide profiles. DS iECs showed increased junctional protein expression and reduced permeability, whereas APPdup iECs displayed increased permeability. Transcriptomic analysis revealed extensive dysregulation in DS iECs, with enrichment of junctional, adhesion, angiogenic, immune, and apoptosis pathways, and reduced cell-cycle, proliferative, and membrane-targeting signatures. APPdup iECs showed milder changes, including impaired protein targeting and reduced adhesion-related pathways. Despite comparable APP dosage, DS iECs maintained greater junctional integrity and lower permeability than APPdup iECs, potentially contributing to differential CAA vulnerability. However, impaired proliferation and altered angiogenesis may reduce BBB resilience during ageing.

title: Algorithmic Geometry Shapes the Biological Meaning of Thalamocortical Structural Covariance
authors: Liu, Y.; Sydnor, V. J.; Dai, A.; Ziolkowski, J.; Fu, S.; Devenyi, G. A.; Satterthwaite, T.; Chakravarty, M.; Yee, Y.
abstract: Neuroimaging studies often derive and discuss structural covariance (SC) as a representation of underlying brain circuitry that reflects coordinated maturation, anatomical connectivity, transcriptional similarity, and shared genetic influences. These associations motivate its use to study brain organization across development, aging, and disease. However, the algorithms used to derive SC networks impose constraints that may shape their biological interpretation. To understand the impact of algorithm choice, we used the thalamocortical system as an example and compared five common representations of voxelwise SC, namely, principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), orthogonal projective NMF (OPNMF), and \textit{k}-means clustering, in 755 participants aged 8--22 years from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC). SC networks derived from deformation-based morphometry (DBM) were evaluated against three complementary biological benchmarks: age-related individual differences, fractional-anisotropy (FA)-based microstructural connectivity of regionally-specific thalamocortical connections, and Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression. Each algorithm demonstrated underlying sensitivity to differing aspects of neurobiology: PCA and OPNMF showed the strongest associations between participant-level component weights and age. NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means showed greater spatial overlap between positive cortical SC and tractography-derived projections. ICA and PCA showed stronger correspondence between thalamic and cortical gene-expression profiles across the transcriptome, whereas NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means more often identified thalamic components with relatively high core-matrix gene expression. This study emphasizes that algorithmic constraints effectively act as biological priors and decomposition methods do not provide neutral compression of the data. We conclude that it is critical to consider whether the algorithmic objective matches the representational geometry of the neurobiology being studied. Overall, our findings suggest that SC studies should select and justify algorithms according to the biological question, explicitly considering whether their constraints favour distributed gradients, overlapping regional parts, or discrete clusters. Meanwhile, interpretations of SC findings could also be informed by the specific algorithmic constraints used to derive them.

title: Item-specific clustering of high gamma-band activity on theta phase during speech categorization
authors: Ten Oever, S.; Reithler, J.; Archila-Melendez, M. E.; Gommer, E.; Rouhl, R.; Kranen-Mastenbroek, V.; Roberts, M. J.; Peters, J.
abstract: Theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been proposed as a mechanism for separating neural representations in time. Although item-specific PAC has been reported, its role in perception remains unclear. Notably, previous work has shown that theta phase can bias perception, raising the question whether such biases are linked to phase-specific gamma activity. Here, we investigated whether phase-dependent perceptual biases are accompanied by item-specific theta-gamma PAC. We presented ambiguous speech sounds that could be interpreted as either /da/ or /ga/ in patients with epilepsy implanted with intracranial electrocorticography. We found that pre-stimulus theta phase predicted both the neural and perceptual response, with /da/ and /ga/ tuned channels exhibiting gamma activity clustering at distinct theta phases. These findings suggest that neural and perceptual biases stem from phase-specific pre-activation of item-specific neural representations. They demonstrate the generalizability of the theta-gamma code, shaping behavior and enhancing representational capacity.

title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease
authors: Qureshi, Y. H.; Guo, J.; Rinald, J. H.; Li, Z.; Soni, R. K.; Govindarajan, A.; Tortora, E.; Uzunova, G.; Yang, Y.; Kannan, S.; Nanayakkara, P.; Troy, C. M.; Small, S. A.
abstract: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. An endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer is pathogenically disrupted in AD. Here we test the hypothesis, that the pathway might drive the neurodegenerative process, via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling SORL1's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, when taken together with other findings the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

title: Generation of human iPSC-derived motor neurons with defined regional identities across the rostrocaudal axis
authors: Ning, K.; Tindel, I.; Singh, B. K.; Zogu, B.; Ho, R.
abstract: This study establishes a unified pipeline for generating human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons (iMNs) with defined hindbrain, cervical, and lumbar identities to support anatomically resolved studies of motor neuron development and degeneration. Conventional differentiation methods can efficiently produce iMNs but provide limited control over rostrocaudal identity and frequently generate populations with heterogeneous HOX profiles. We addressed this limitation by optimizing developmental morphogen combinations and treatment windows, establishing three complementary protocols that reproducibly generated hindbrain/rhombomere-associated motor neurons (RiMNs), cervical motor neurons (CiMNs), and lumbar motor neurons (LiMNs) across iPSC lines from six non-diseased donors balanced by sex. Transcriptomic and protein analyses demonstrated graded rostrocaudal specification from RiMNs through CiMNs to LiMNs, together with region-appropriate motor neuron subtype features. These identities showed the expected relationships to human week 9 fetal rostrocaudal HOX programs. High-density multielectrode array analysis further revealed synchronized network firing, electrically active neurite networks, and enhanced axonal signal propagation in the regional iMN populations compared with conventionally differentiated iMNs. Spike-sorted recordings additionally revealed protocol-associated differences in single-neuron electrophysiological profiles. Together, this three-protocol pipeline enables the reproducible generation and comparative analysis of anatomically defined human motor neuron populations and provides region-matched cellular models for investigating motor neuron development, selective degeneration, and therapeutic responses.

title: Brain representations of visual short-term memories during healthy human aging: occipital decline and frontoparietal compensation
authors: Mitchell, D. J.; Cam-CAN,  ; Cusack, R.
abstract: Visual short-term memory declines steeply with age, but the link to neural representations of memory content remains unknown. We used fMRI decoding to relate remembered motion-direction representations in visual and frontoparietal cortex to age and performance, in 115 adults, aged 25-87, from the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) cohort. Decoding was strongest in visual cortex, but also significant in frontoparietal regions, with different profiles. Visual representations weakened with memory load and age, and statistically mediated age-related performance decline, especially during recall. This coupling, however, weakened with age: some older adults retained stronger visual representations than performance implied, suggesting impaired access to a partially preserved memory trace. Frontoparietal representations, instead, were largely insensitive to load and strengthened with age during maintenance, partially offsetting performance decline. Therefore, interventions to boost VSTM in older adults might target compensatory frontoparietal representations during memory maintenance, and readout of untapped visual representations at recall.

title: The Alzheimer's disease-associated rs28834970 variant in PTK2B impairs electrical activity and regulates Tau phosphorylation and APP processing in human neuronal cultures
authors: Lannette-Weimann, N.; Huyvaert, M.; Limoge, F.; Lemaire, M.; Gao, V.; Maurier, F.; Guyot, K.; Henocq, C.; Coulon, A.; Buiche, V.; Rabiller, F.; Majernikova, N.; Walle, P.; Desnoulez-Salome, S.; Neiva-Queiros, B.; Lopez-Perez, P.; Morita Miyakoshi, L.; Melo de Farias, A. R.; Costa, M. R.; Amouyel, P.; Najdek, C.; Dannert, A.; Gonzalez-Gallego, J.; Muntaner, M.; Grenier-Boley, B.; Chapuis, J.; Paquet, D.; Kilinc, D. R.; Lambert, J.-C.; Dumont, J.
abstract: Background: Genome-wide association studies have identified the PTK2B gene, which encodes Proline-rich tyrosine kinase 2 (PYK2), as a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, its role in AD aetiology remains to be understood, as a complex contribution to amyloid {beta} (A{beta}) toxicity, tauopathy and neuronal dysfunction is suggested by contradictory evidence. Determining how the causal variant among AD-associated PTK2B variants impairs PYK2 function to trigger AD hallmarks could bring clarification. Methods: We combined in silico prediction tools with luciferase reporter assays in neuroblastoma cells to prioritize potential AD-associated PTK2B functional variants. We generated isogenic KOLF2.1J induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) carrying the most relevant functional variant using CRISPR-Cas9 and differentiated them into human neuronal cultures (hNCs). We assessed PYK2 expression via immunoblotting, performed transcriptomic profiling using RNA-sequencing, analyzed neuronal network activity via multielectrode array (MEA) recordings, quantified synaptic density through immunocytochemistry in microfluidic devices, and assessed Tau phosphorylation and amyloid-precursor protein (APP) metabolism. Results: The rs28834970 regulatory variant was identified as the most functionally relevant in our model, with the C risk allele promoting transcription factor C/EBP{beta} binding within a cis-regulatory element. In hNCs, the homozygous rs28834970 CC genotype reduced total PYK2 levels by more than 80%, while increasing the proportion of phosphorylated (activated) PYK2. Transcriptomic analysis revealed 724 downregulated and 113 upregulated gene sets, with altered expression of genes involved in extracellular matrix organization, cytoplasmic translation and neurotransmitter secretion. MEA recordings showed reduced network recruitment and altered burst organization. Immunocytochemistry in microfluidic devices consistently revealed that rs28834970 impacts dendritic development and postsynaptic maturation. The risk genotype significantly elevated Tau phosphorylation at pathological sites (Thr181, Thr217, Thr231, Ser202-Thr205, Ser396-Ser404), and enhanced APP processing, resulting in decreased levels of APP and CTF but increased levels of sAPP, sAPP{beta} and A{beta}. Conclusion: The rs28834970 C risk allele mechanistically links AD susceptibility to downregulation of PTK2B/PYK2 expression and to the increase in Tau pathology and A{beta} levels while compromising synaptic structure and function.

title: A novel function of neuroligin 3: Beyond sociality, Regulating lifespan in Drosophila
authors: Kurbaj, J. M.; Ataei, R.; Simon, A. F.
abstract: Neuroligins are conserved postsynaptic adhesion proteins involved in synaptic function and behaviour. In Drosophila melanogaster, Neuroligin 3 (Nlg3) regulates social behaviour, sleep and synaptic architecture. We now report, through analysis of publicly available transcriptomics data, confirmed with RT-qPCR data, that loss-of-function of the nlg3 gene downregulates the expression of longevity-associated genes foxo, hsp70s, and hsp68. Graded genetic manipulation of the Drosophila melanogaster neuroligin 3 (nlg3) gene indeed modulates both social spacing and lifespan. Specifically, reduced nlg3 expression (via heterozygous deletion, or transposable-element insertion) extends lifespan in both sexes, while overexpression or complete deletion shortens it. In contrast, overexpression or complete loss of nlg3 leads the flies to be further apart (increased social distance, or social space), as does RNAi knockdown, while heterozygous reduction of nlg3 expression either lowers or does not alter the flies social space. This work identifies a previously unrecognized link between a conserved synaptic gene, social behaviour, and organismal longevity.

title: Emergence of Task-Related Motor Cortical Dysfunction in Mice with Progressive Parkinsonism
authors: Chehade, H. D.; Berezhnoi, D.; Somavarapu, S.; Wang, Z.; Jiang, J.; Chen, L.; Risk, B. B.; Wichmann, T.; Chu, H.-Y.
abstract: The primary motor cortex (M1) exhibits substantial changes in Parkinsons disease (PD). However, the temporal relationship between midbrain dopamine (DA) neurodegeneration, M1 circuit dysfunction, and motor symptoms remains poorly understood. Using the MitoPark mice, we investigated the time course of M1 cellular dysfunction during progressive DA loss. MitoPark mice developed gradually impaired skilled movements at a moderate motor stage of Parkinsonism. The motor deficits were associated with reduced cellular activity, impaired neuronal coactivation, and decreased proportion of responsive M1 pyramidal neurons. Moreover, the corticospinal (CSp), but not the intratelencephalic (IT), neurons showed a selective reduction in cellular activity during reaches. At the population level, M1 pyramidal neurons included heterogeneous functional clusters in relation to skilled movements and their stability in longitudinal encoding of movement degraded substantially in MitoPark mice. Together, these results delineate the emergence of M1 circuit pathophysiology at cellular and neural population levels during progressive Parkinsonism.

title: Determining Reliable Neural Targets for enhancing Motor Sequence Learning: A preparatory study for focal tDCS
authors: Khan, A.; Burke, M.; Genc, E.; CHHABRA, H.; Kuo, M.-F.; Nitsche, M.
abstract: Background: Motor sequence learning (MSL) underlies the acquisition of everyday skilled movements, and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has shown promise for enhancing it, although reported effects vary considerably. Before such interventions can be applied and interpreted reliably, the behavioural and neural signatures of the underlying task should be shown to be robust. This study therefore characterised an fMRI-based Serial Reaction Time Task (SRTT) protocol and evaluated the consistency of its behavioural and fMRI-based neural signatures in repeated measurements to identify potential network targets for tDCS. Methods: Twenty healthy young- to middle-aged adults (10 females; mean age 24, SD 4) performed the SRTT during 3T fMRI in two sessions about one week apart, each using one of two matched, non-overlapping task versions in counterbalanced order. We examined block-wise behaviour, task-related and sequence-specific brain activation (general task activation relative to baseline and the SEQ > RND contrast), and functional connectivity using two complementary approaches: the task and temporal dynamics of seed-based connectivity (SBC) within an a priori defined motor network (M1, SMA, PMC, putamen, and cerebellum), and whole brain generalised psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) for the SEQ > RND contrast. Results: Reaction time decreased steadily across sequence blocks and returned toward baseline during random blocks, confirming implicit sequence learning; this pattern was consistent across both sessions and both task versions. Test retest reliability was excellent for random-block reaction time (ICC = 80 to .85), and modest for sequence blocks (ICC = .29 to.53). General task activation (sequence and random performance relative to baseline) engaged the expected sensorimotor network, including the primary motor cortex (M1), premotor cortex, and SMA, with M1 more strongly engaged during sequence than random blocks. The sequence-specific contrast (SEQ > RND) additionally revealed six clusters spanning the left superior parietal cortex, bilateral supplementary and cingulate motor areas, bilateral secondary somatosensory cortex, and left ventral visual cortex together with cerebellar Crus I. The a priori defined motor network was engaged across all task phases and was anchored throughout by strong M1 to SMA coupling, with overall network coupling following a non-monotonic course across the session, consistent with successive stages of resource allocation, consolidation, and automatisation. The gPPI analysis identified four sequence-specific connectivity clusters, dominated by a right-lateralised visuomotor network and a somatosensory visual integration channel. Conclusions: Together, these findings indicate a two-component architecture for SRTT performance: a left hemispheric cortico striato cerebellar network that supports performance and acquisition of the sequence, and a right hemispheric network associated with monitoring its predictable structure. Within this protocol, the SRTT produced robust and stable group-level signatures of implicit motor learning, yielding well-defined network targets for future tDCS interventions..

title: Contextual encoding of states and indices for episodic memories make goal-directed action selection flexible, transparent, and efficient
authors: Yang, Y.; Maass, W.
abstract: When we want to solve a problem, our brain helps us by recalling related experiences. Furthermore, it can selectively recall only those experiences that fit especially well to the current context and contingencies. In addition, it provides explanations for chosen actions in terms of prior experiences. We show that experimental data on underlying neural codes of the brain, in particular contextual encoding of states and index cells for episodic memories, enable us to port essential aspects of the problem solving strategy of the brain into a simple algorithm. It only requires local online learning in shallow neural networks with low resolution of synaptic weights in order to explore a new environment, and it supports low-latency decision making. Hence it is especially suited for implementation in edge devices. Surprisingly, the performance of this light-weight algorithm on a standard benchmark task, navigation in Markov Decision Processes, is competitive with that of commonly used but computationally more demanding, less flexible, and less transparent reinforcement learning approaches.

title: Toward defining loss functions in neuroscience: an XOR-based neuronal mechanism for local learning
authors: Pena Fernandez, M.; Lloret Iglesias, L.; Marco de Lucas, J.
abstract: Of the three components often used to map deep learning onto neuroscience (architecture, learning rule and loss function), the biological counterpart of the loss is the least understood. For binary signals, the mismatch between an externally evoked response and its internally generated reconstruction is the XOR function, and its two asymmetric components, undershoot and overshoot, form a signed error that also indicates the direction of the required change. In a companion study, an eight-neuron, Dale-compliant signed-XOR motif, a six-neuron XOR comparator with two feedback neurons of opposite identity, was found in several connectomes and shown in spiking simulations to compute this signed error. Here we ask whether this signed error can serve as an effective learning signal. We use the logical function of one comparator per output unit as the only error signal of a binary autoencoder, with fixed random sign feedback to the hidden layer. Without backpropagation, a fully connected autoencoder trained for five epochs on binarized MNIST reaches 97.7% bit-wise and 94.8% balanced reconstruction accuracy (five seeds), and a convolutional variant with 533 parameters reaches 96.3% and 89.2%; without the sign of the error, learning collapses. Controls show that performance is carried by the comparator-driven decoder: a suitably initialised fixed random encoder reconstructs digits about as well or better, encoder learning improves digit readout mainly in narrow hidden layers, and a gradient-trained reference reaches 99.3% and 97.3% balanced accuracy. The signed error thus suffices for the synapses it reaches directly; credit assignment to earlier layers remains open.

title: Lexical surprisal drives pupil dilation during continuous story listening
authors: Terzo, C.; Berlot, E.; de Lange, F.
abstract: The pupil famously adjusts its dilation in response to light, but its role extends far beyond this basic sensory function. Its fluctuations index arousal and mental effort, beyond luminance-related dynamics, making it a sensitive marker of internal cognitive states. A growing body of work shows that these pupil-linked signals extend beyond the visual domain. However, which processes drive pupil responses in more naturalistic settings remains unclear as most evidence comes from tightly controlled paradigms that strip away the richness of real-world experience. Language offers a uniquely powerful window into this question, as it can allow us to create rich paradigms without having any visual, i.e. luminance, confounds. Moreover, language comprehension hinges on continuous prediction: listeners constantly generate expectations about upcoming input, and the discrepancy between expectation and actual input - contextual prediction error, or surprisal - carries measurable cognitive costs. Here, we tested the hypothesis that pupil-linked arousal indexes these linguistic surprisal signals during naturalistic listening. We recorded pupil responses while volunteers listened to naturalistic spoken stories in darkness, which were either intact or reversed. Reversed speech preserves the acoustics of the signal while destroying its intelligibility. Pupil dilation selectively tracked lexical surprisal within a late window of 1,700 to 2,350 milliseconds following word onset, in forward, but not control, backward speech. These findings indicate that pupil-linked arousal is tuned to global, context-dependent processing, tracking the cognitive cost of updating a predictive model during naturalistic listening.

title: Salience network expansion as a transdiagnostic neural marker for psychopathology risk in adolescence
authors: Koirala, S.; Hermosillo, R.; Godfrey, K. J.; Anderson, M.; Lundquist, J.; Moser, J.; Feczko, E.; Miranda Dominguez, O.; Weldon, K. B.; Linder, I.; Mahmoudi, M.; Uddin, L. Q.; Nelson, S. M.; Elison, J. T.; Fair, D.; Tervo-Clemmens, B.
abstract: Increased cortical surface area of the brain's salience network (SAL) has been observed in depression and appears to emerge during early adolescence. However, similar expansion has also been reported in bipolar disorder (BD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and other atypicalities of salience network function have been broadly implicated across multiple psychiatric conditions. Whether increased SAL surface area is specific to depression or related more generally with psychopathology remains unclear. Using data collected as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (baseline: N = 7942; ages 9-10; Year 2: N = 5901; ages 11-12), we quantified individual SAL size and examined associations with dimensional symptoms from the Child Behavior Checklist. SAL surface area showed substantial inter-individual variability, with expansion occurring primarily through encroachment into the default mode (DMN), action-mode (AMN), and frontoparietal (FP) networks. Larger SAL size showed a modest positive association with depressive symptoms in the baseline sample, consistent with prior reports; however, this association did not replicate in the year 2 internal replication sample. Instead, associations with total problems were stronger and replicated across both timepoints, suggesting a subtle, dimensional relationship between SAL organization and general psychopathology burden. These findings suggest that individual differences in SAL organization may represent a broader transdiagnostic neural correlate of dimensional psychopathology rather than a disorder-specific neural signature.

title: Lipid Changes due to Low O-GlcNAc and the Downstream Consequences
authors: Fei, G. Q.; Marando, V. M.; Olszewski, K. L.; Gibbs, B. E.; Jensen, W. G.; Hall, A. M. J.; Jost, M.; Walker, S.
abstract: O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is an essential mammalian glycosyltransferase that installs O-GlcNAc onto thousands of cytosolic and nuclear proteins. Dysregulated glycosylation by OGT is associated with disease states, including cancer and neurodegeneration. However, cellular consequences of acute loss of O-GlcNAc remain poorly understood. Here, we employed a cell-permeable small molecule inhibitor of OGT, OSMI-4, coupled with transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses to characterize the effects of O-GlcNAc depletion in human cell lines. Loss of O-GlcNAc led to changes in expression of lipid metabolism genes and remodeling of the lipidome, with unsaturated phosphatidylcholines (PCs), saturated lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) and unsaturated storage lipids accumulating. We also observed increased lipid droplets. Our results suggest that polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) accumulate in the membrane under low O-GlcNAc conditions and that cells buffer this accumulation by removing PUFAs from membrane lipids and sequestering them in lipid droplets. We found that treatment with OSMI-4 sensitizes cells to ferroptosis inducers, likely because accumulated cell membrane PUFAs undergo peroxidation. Taken together, our results highlight lipid remodeling as an important process that mediates the downstream effects of loss of O-GlcNAc. It may be possible to exploit the synergy between OGT inhibitors and ferroptosis inducers for therapeutic benefit.

title: iPSC modeling of pulmonary arterial hypertension to uncover pathomechanisms and unrecognized modes of action of sotatercept
authors: Schmidt, A.; czichon, L.; Malhofer, L.; Bartsch, G.; Ploetner, C.; Wang, Y.; Voss, C.; Kuleshova, A. E.; Kohrn, T.; Baldauf, J.; Weiss, A.; Schermuly, R.; Ruhparwar, A.; Kamp, J.-C.; Hoeper, M.; Martin, U.; Olmer, R.
abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a potentially fatal disease characterized by obliterative remodeling of distal pulmonary arteries, commonly associated with bone morphogenetic receptor type 2 (BMPR2) gene mutations. In patients with PAH, sotatercept, an activin signaling inhibitor, improves hemodynamics and outcomes, but clinical responses vary ranging from rapid improvements within weeks to no clinical benefit, suggesting additional mechanisms beyond its anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects. Using patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived smooth muscle cells (iSMCs) with BMPR2 extracellular- or kinase-domain mutations, we reproduced Activin A-driven PAH traits, including hyperproliferation, reduced apoptosis, enhanced contraction and excessive matrix production. We identified smooth muscle cell-to-myofibroblast transition as a previously unknown contributor to pulmonary vascular remodeling and demonstrated its inhibition by sotatercept. Beyond its established effects, sotatercept rapidly reduced contractility, collagen-integrin mechanotransduction and TGFbeta receptor expression, disrupting a pathological positive feedback loop, reflected by lower levels of circulating TGFbeta1 in patients on sotatercept. Taken together, our patient-derived iSMC platform links mutation-dependent mechanisms of pulmonary vascular remodeling to variable drug responsiveness and reveals previously unrecognized, potentially rapid-acting modes of sotatercept in PAH.

title: mTOR signalling, not clock gene rhythms, organises daily physiology
authors: Zeng, A.; Mihut, A.; Anandapadamanaban, M.; Goity, A.; de Barros Dantas, L. L.; Peak Chew, S.-Y.; Hayter, E. A.; Andersson, L. C.; Smith, T.; Pasquini, G.; Seinkmane, E.; Stangherlin, A.; James, N. R.; Beresford, C.; Farnsworth, J.; Menzies, J.; al-Rawi, A.; Holt, L. J.; Derivery, E.; Edgar, R. S.; Madsen, R. R.; Bechtold, D. A.; Larrondo, L. F.; Dodd, A. N.; Rihel, J.; Ratto, G. M.; Williams, J.; Newham, P.; Hilgendorf, C.; Beale, A. D.; Lodovichi, C.; O'Neill, J. S.
abstract: Daily rhythms in mammalian physiology are widely attributed to rhythmic transcription of "clock-controlled genes" driven by the circadian transcriptional/translational feedback loop (TTFL). Here we show that daily physiology can be uncoupled from the TTFL: inhibiting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) abolishes most daily variation in cellular and organismal physiology, whilst clock protein rhythms persist. In cultured cells and mouse liver, functional rhythms are lost, including the proteome, RNA abundance, substrate utilisation and drug metabolism. In forebrain, most daily variation in protein abundance and phosphorylation is lost, yet locomotor activity and sleep-wake architecture are largely preserved in mice and zebrafish. PERIOD2 binds mTORC1 and limits its activity, providing a route by which clock proteins shape daily mTOR signalling. mTOR inhibition preferentially suppresses output over clock gene rhythms in Arabidopsis and Neurospora. We conclude that mTOR is a conserved conduit through which circadian and environmental timing impose daily organisation on physiology.

title: Knockdown of the long non-coding RNA DNAAF3-AS1 activates the p53 pathway and remodels the H3K36me3 landscape
authors: Budkina, A.; Zubritskiy, A.; Marakulina, D.; Buyan, A.; Kulakovsky, I.; Yip, C. W.; Aneke, J.; Shin, J.; Medvedeva, Y. A.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs are increasingly recognised as chromatin regulators, yet most remain functionally uncharacterised. DNAAF3-AS1, transcribed antisense to the ciliary dynein assembly factor gene DNAAF3, is almost exclusively associated with H3K36me3 in the HiMoRNA database. H3K36me3 ChIP-seq in human dermal fibroblasts following DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown with two independent antisense oligonucleotides revealed a marked reduction of gene-body H3K36me3, with residual signal shifted towards promoters. In FANTOM6 CAGE, DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown activated the p53 pathway and triggered differential promoter usage in genes enriched for p53 and apoptotic regulators. Consistently, genes that gained gene-body H3K36me3 upon knockdown were enriched for apoptosis-related pathways. In line with high expression of DNAAF3-AS1 in testis, analysis based on the adult human testis single-cell atlas suggests that DNAAF3-AS1 may contribute to promoter-level H3K36me3 regulation during late spermatogenesis. Together, these results identify DNAAF3-AS1 as a chromatin-associated lncRNA that links H3K36me3 maintenance to p53 signalling.
